name: Vector as list and arrow
statement: A vector in R^2 is two things at once — a list of two numbers and an arrow from the origin — and the two readings stay in step because addition (componentwise, tip-to-tail) and scalar multiplication (componentwise, stretching) behave identically in each reading.
aliases: a list of two numbers, and an arrow from the origin

name: Coordinates as axis recipe
statement: Every vector (x, y) equals x·e1 + y·e2 for the axis vectors e1 = (1,0) and e2 = (0,1); a vector's coordinates are not a label attached to it but its recipe in terms of the axes — x steps east, y steps north.
aliases: Every vector is a recipe out of those two

name: Parallel directions
statement: Two vectors are parallel exactly when one is a scalar multiple of the other; a nonzero 2×2 determinant says exactly that the two directions are not parallel.

name: Independence of two vectors
statement: If u and v are not parallel, then au + bv = a'u + b'v forces a = a' and b = b': rearranging gives (a−a')u = (b'−b)v, and a nonzero multiple of u cannot equal a multiple of v unless both sides are zero. Perpendicularity plays no role in this.

name: Slanted coordinate grid
statement: Two non-parallel vectors u and v form a coordinate system for the plane: every point has exactly one representation a·u + b·v, read off a slanted grid of parallelograms that becomes a square grid only when the directions are perpendicular — non-perpendicularity does not break the coordinate system, it only makes the cells slanted.
aliases: perpendicularity is a convenience, not a requirement

name: Parallel collapse to a line
statement: If v is a scalar multiple of u, the set of all combinations a·u + b·v is a single line: points on that line have infinitely many representations and points off it have none.

name: Determinant, parallelism, invertibility
statement: A 2×2 matrix has determinant zero exactly when its two columns are parallel; a nonzero determinant means the columns are not parallel and the map is invertible, so every target vector has exactly one preimage.

name: Determinant-zero collapse
statement: When a 2×2 matrix has determinant zero, it squashes the whole plane onto a line — the geometric face of rank deficiency.

name: Linear map
statement: A map L is linear when it respects the two vector operations: L(u + v) = L(u) + L(v) and L(cu) = c·L(u) — add then map gives the same answer as map then add, and scale then map gives the same as map then scale; this is the whole requirement.

name: Not bending the grid
statement: Linearity is the algebraic form of not bending the grid: a linear map sends straight lines to straight lines, keeps parallel lines parallel, keeps even spacing even, and can only rotate, stretch, shear, flatten or reflect — never fold or bend.
aliases: the maps that don't bend the grid

name: Linear maps fix the origin
statement: Every linear map fixes the origin: L(0) = L(0 + 0) = L(0) + L(0) forces L(0) = 0, so any map that moves the origin is not linear.

name: Axis determination
statement: A linear map is completely pinned down by where it sends the two standard axes: L(x, y) = x·L(e1) + y·L(e2), because the axis recipe is the unique way to build a vector and linearity lets the map distribute over that sum and pull the scalars out — every other value is forced arithmetic, not a further choice.
aliases: A linear map is completely pinned down by where it sends the axes

name: Columns are axis images
statement: The columns of a matrix are exactly the images of the standard axes under the linear map it represents — first column L(e1), second column L(e2) — and that is what the numbers are, not an interpretation added on top; so reading a matrix off is reading where the axes land, with no computation required.
aliases: The columns are where the axes land
Reading a matrix is reading where the axes land

name: Matrix-vector product as column combination
statement: Multiplying a matrix by a vector means taking the linear combination of that matrix's columns weighted by the vector's entries: A(x, y) = x·col1 + y·col2 — take x copies of the first column, y copies of the second, add them.
aliases: A x is a weighted mix of the columns

name: Row-dot rule
statement: The row-dotted-with-the-vector rule computes the same thing as the column combination, only grouped differently: the k-th entry of x·col1 + y·col2 is row k dotted with the input, so the row view is a fast way to compute while the column view is the one that carries the meaning.

name: Eigenvector and eigenvalue
statement: An eigenvector of a linear map is a direction the map does not knock off its line, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the factor by which the map stretches, shrinks or flips vectors along that direction — not a multiplication by 1.
aliases: directions the map doesn't knock off their line

name: Eigendecomposition
statement: In its own eigenvector coordinates, a linear map with a full set of eigenvectors is a pure stretch along each coordinate axis — that is its eigendecomposition.

name: Least squares as projection
statement: Least-squares fitting of Ax ≈ b is the orthogonal projection of b onto the column space of A.

name: PCA directions
statement: The principal directions found by PCA are the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix of the data — the directions in which the data varies most.

name: Singular value decomposition
statement: Every matrix factors as a rotation, then a stretch, then another rotation — the singular value decomposition — which is the eigendecomposition idea applied to AᵀA.
aliases: every matrix is rotate · stretch · rotate

name: Rank-k truncation
statement: Rank-k truncation keeps only the k largest singular components of a matrix, and this is what dimensionality reduction beyond PCA consists in.

name: Matrix multiplication as composition
statement: The matrix product BA represents the composite map "apply A first, then B", and its j-th column is B applied to the j-th column of A — because the j-th column of A is where A sends the j-th axis vector, and the composite must then send that image onward through B. Multiplying matrices is composing the maps they represent, nothing more.
aliases: the columns record one path through the two maps

name: Shear and quarter turn do not commute
statement: For the shear A = [[1,1],[0,1]] and the quarter turn B = [[0,−1],[1,0]], shearing then rotating gives BA = [[0,−1],[1,1]] while rotating then shearing gives AB = [[1,−1],[1,0]]: the same two maps applied in the two orders produce genuinely different matrices, since e1 goes 1→0→1 in the first order and 0→1→1 in the second while e2 goes 0→1→(−1,1) versus (−1,0)→(−1,0).

name: Non-commutativity
statement: Matrix multiplication is not commutative, AB ≠ BA in general, and the reason is geometric rather than a quirk of notation: the columns of a product record a path through the two maps, and two different orders of the same maps are two different paths with different outcomes.

name: Row-dot-column entry rule
statement: The (k, j) entry of a product BA is row k of B dotted with column j of A — the familiar "rows times columns" computation is exactly the composition rule read entry by entry, not a separate definition.

name: Zero product from nonzero factors
statement: A product of matrices AB can be the zero matrix even when neither A nor B is zero, because composing transformations allows one map to flatten the plane onto a line and the next to send that line to the origin — the algebraic oddity is just rank loss under composition.
aliases: AB = 0 is possible with neither factor zero

name: Span
statement: The span of a set of vectors is the set of all linear combinations of it — everything that can be built from it — and it is always a subspace through the origin: in the plane a point, a line or the whole plane, in R^3 a point, a line, a plane or all of space. A span is made of sums, not unions: the span of two non-parallel directions is the entire plane, including points that lie on neither line.

name: Linear independence
statement: A set of vectors is linearly independent when no vector in it can be built as a combination of the others — each contributes a direction the rest cannot supply; otherwise the set is dependent and its extra vectors are pure redundancy.

name: Basis and coordinates
statement: A basis is a set that is both independent and spanning — exactly enough vectors, no waste and no gaps; with respect to any basis, slanted or perpendicular, every point has exactly one recipe as a combination of the basis vectors, so coordinates are not intrinsic to a point but a description relative to a chosen basis — which is what makes a change of basis a move one can make at all.

name: Dependence test
statement: A set of vectors is dependent exactly when some non-trivial linear combination of it equals the zero vector; this algebraic test replaces eyeballing and reveals precisely which vectors are redundant.

name: Kernel as a subspace
statement: The kernel (null space) of a linear map A is the set of inputs it sends to zero, and it is always a subspace through the origin: if Ax = 0 and Ay = 0 then A(x + y) = 0, so kernels are closed under linear combination rather than being a random scatter of vectors.

name: Column space and rank
statement: For an m×n matrix, the reachable outputs are exactly the span of its columns — the column space — and the rank equals the number of independent columns, the dimension of the column space, i.e. how many dimensions of output the map actually reaches; Ax = b is solvable exactly when b lies in the column space, and nothing else governs solvability.

name: Rank–nullity
statement: Rank–nullity: rank + dim(ker A) = n for an m×n matrix — the dimensions of output reached plus the dimensions destroyed equal the dimension of the input, a conservation law.

name: Invertibility criterion
statement: For an n×n matrix A: A is invertible iff rank = n iff ker A = {0} iff det A ≠ 0 — an inverse exists exactly when nothing is lost, which is what computing a determinant is really testing.

name: Solution set as particular plus kernel
statement: If x is one solution of Ax = b, the full solution set is x plus the entire kernel: two solutions differ by a kernel vector, so the solutions are one particular solution plus a line (or plane) of sliding freedom.

name: Rank is not the column count
statement: The number of vectors says nothing about how much they span; only the number of independent directions matters, so rank answers 'how many solutions', never 'how many columns'. With three or more vectors dependence is usually a sum with assorted coefficients, invisible to the eye, and elimination detects it: the number of pivots in row echelon form is the rank, and a row of zeros is the signature of dependence.

name: Dot product as alignment
statement: u·v = Σ u_i v_i = ‖u‖‖v‖ cos θ: the sum-of-products is forced, not conventional, by applying the law of cosines to the triangle with sides u, v and u − v — the geometric and coordinate expansions of ‖u − v‖² agree on the squared lengths ‖u‖² and ‖v‖², so the leftover terms must agree, giving x₁y₁ + x₂y₂ = ‖u‖‖v‖ cos θ.

name: Consequences of the dot product identity
statement: From u·v = ‖u‖‖v‖cos θ: u·v = 0 exactly when the vectors are perpendicular or one is zero, so orthogonality is expressed as an equation; length comes free as ‖u‖ = √(u·u); and the sign reports whether the vectors lean the same way (positive) or opposed (negative), the magnitude reporting how strongly. In high-dimensional spaces such as 768-dimensional embeddings there is no picture of the angle, so cos θ = u·v/(‖u‖‖v‖) is the only definition of angle available, which is why cosine similarity is the standard similarity measure there and raw dot products must be normalized before comparison.

name: Projection formula
statement: The projection of v onto the direction u is proj_u v = (u·v / u·u) u: the coefficient c is forced by requiring the remainder v − c·u to be perpendicular to u, i.e. (v − c·u)·u = 0. The numerator measures how much of v lies along u and the denominator measures how long u is, since a long u must be stepped in smaller fractions to cover the same ground; when u is a unit vector the coefficient collapses to u·v.

name: Projection as closest point
statement: The projection c·u is the closest point on the line spanned by u: since v − c·u is perpendicular to u, Pythagoras gives ‖v − w‖² = ‖v − c·u‖² + ‖c·u − w‖² for any point w on the line, which is smallest exactly at w = c·u — the seed of least squares.

name: Projection matrix
statement: Projection onto the direction u is itself a linear map with matrix P = u·uᵀ / (uᵀu); reading its columns shows it sends u to itself and everything perpendicular to u to zero, so it keeps one line and destroys another — its rank is 1 and it is not invertible.

name: Eigenvector equation
statement: An eigenvector v of A with eigenvalue λ satisfies A·v = λ·v with v ≠ 0, equivalently (A − λI)·v = 0: eigenvectors are exactly the nonzero vectors in the kernel of A − λI, so finding them means finding the directions that A − λI collapses.

name: Composition order
statement: Three maps applied in the order A, then B, then C compose to the matrix product CBA — the rightmost factor acts first, because that is the one the input's coordinates travel through first.

name: Eigenvalues are singularity values
statement: Eigenvalues are exactly the values of λ for which A − λI is singular: the eigenvector equation (A − λI)v = 0 with v ≠ 0 says a nonzero vector is being destroyed, i.e. A − λI has a nontrivial kernel, and an invertible matrix kills only 0 and so could never be A − λI.
aliases: eigenvalues are the values of λ that make A − λI singular

name: Characteristic equation
statement: The characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0: computing the determinant with λ left symbolic gives the characteristic polynomial, whose roots are the eigenvalues, turning the abstract property 'not invertible' into a solvable equation in one unknown; once λ is fixed, its eigenvectors are the kernel of the now-singular matrix A − λI.

name: Trace and determinant checks
statement: For a 2×2 matrix the characteristic polynomial is λ² − tr(A)λ + det(A), so its eigenvalues sum to the trace and multiply to the determinant — two free arithmetic checks on any eigenvalue computation.

name: Complex and repeated eigenvalues
statement: A real matrix can have complex eigenvalues — a 90° rotation has only ±i and no real ones — and eigenvalues can repeat, so two distinct real roots cannot be expected in general.
